title: Electric Sync
subtitle: Sync Postgres into local clients over HTTP with Shapes
throughline: One projects row, from Postgres through a Shape and the shape log into a local TanStack DB collection, then written back through your own API.

chapters.title: What is a Shape
chapters.blurb: A Shape is a table plus an optional where clause and an optional columns subset, defining the little slice of Postgres you sync.

story.title: What is a Shape
story.subtitle: Sync Postgres into local clients over HTTP with Shapes

steps.title: What is a Shape
steps.narration: A **Shape** is the core primitive for controlling sync in Electric: a defined subset of your Postgres data.
steps.say: Electric syncs little subsets of Postgres into local apps, and the primitive that defines a subset is called a shape.
steps.coverSubtitle: A table, an optional where clause, an optional columns subset

steps.title: Too much to sync
steps.narration: Imagine a **Postgres** database in the cloud with lots of data. Syncing all of it onto a local device is often impractical or unwanted.
steps.say: Picture a Postgres database in the cloud holding a lot of data. Syncing every row of it down to a local device is usually impractical, and most of the time you don't even want it.

steps.title: Start with a table
steps.narration: Every shape must specify a **table** that matches a table in Postgres, such as `projects`. Bare names default to the `public.` schema.
steps.say: So you define a subset. Every shape starts from a single table that has to match a real table in Postgres, here the projects table. A bare name like that is assumed to live in the public schema.

steps.title: An optional where clause
steps.narration: Add an optional **where clause** to filter which rows are included, like `status IN ('backlog', 'todo')`. Only matching rows join the shape.
steps.say: Next, an optional where clause filters which rows are included. You write it as a normal Postgres expression, for example status in backlog or todo, and only the rows that match end up in the shape.

steps.title: An optional columns subset
steps.narration: An optional **columns** clause selects which columns sync, e.g. `columns=id,title,status`. It must always include the primary key.
steps.say: You can also narrow the shape sideways with an optional columns clause, choosing just the columns you want, like id, title and status. The one rule is that the selection must always include the primary key.

steps.title: The shape is a subset
steps.narration: Together the **Shape** is a table plus optional filters: a precise subset of Postgres. Many clients can sync the same shape and shapes can overlap.
steps.say: Put those together and the shape is the table, the optional where clause, and the optional columns, defining one precise subset of Postgres. Many clients can sync the same shape, and shapes are allowed to overlap.

steps.title: Single table and immutable
steps.narration: A shape is *single table* and its definition is *immutable*: once a subscription starts, you can't change it; you start a new one instead.
steps.say: Two things to remember about a shape. It covers a single table, and its definition is immutable. Once a subscription has started you can't edit it, so to change the data you sync you simply start a new shape.

chapters.title: The Shape Log over HTTP
chapters.blurb: Clients consume a shape as an ordered log of inserts, updates and deletes over GET /v1/shape, then tail it live.

story.title: The Shape Log over HTTP
story.subtitle: Sync Postgres into local clients over HTTP with Shapes

steps.title: The Shape Log over HTTP
steps.narration: Syncing a shape gives you a **Shape Log**: an ordered log of logical operations, consumed over the `GET /v1/shape` endpoint.
steps.say: When you sync a shape you don't get a snapshot, you get a log. An ordered shape log of database operations, served over a single HTTP endpoint.
steps.coverSubtitle: GET /v1/shape, an offset, a handle, then tail it live

steps.title: The initial sync request
steps.narration: A client makes an initial request to `GET /v1/shape` with `table=projects` and `offset=-1`, asking for the whole log from the start.
steps.say: It starts with an initial sync request. The client calls get slash v1 slash shape, passing the table parameter set to projects and an offset of minus one. That minus one means give me the whole log, from the very start of this shape.

steps.title: Postgres populates the log
steps.narration: On first request Electric queries **Postgres** and turns the results into insert operations, building the **Shape Log** the endpoint streams back.
steps.say: When a shape is first requested, Electric queries Postgres and turns the matching rows into insert operations. That builds the shape log, an ordered record of changes that the endpoint then streams back.

steps.title: Inserts, updates, deletes
steps.narration: Each shape log entry carries a `value` and an `action` header — `insert`, `update` or `delete`. The client replays them to materialize the shape.
steps.say: Each entry in the log carries a value and an action header that says whether it's an insert, an update, or a delete. The client's job is to replay those operations in order to materialize the current value of the shape.

steps.title: The up-to-date message
steps.narration: At the end of the data the server sends a control message `{ "headers": { "control": "up-to-date" } }`, meaning the client now has everything the server knew.
steps.say: When the client has read everything the server currently knows about, the endpoint sends a control message marked up to date. That's the signal that the initial sync is complete and the local copy of the shape is current.

steps.title: Switch into live mode
steps.narration: Now the client tails the shape with `live=true`, the current `offset` and the shape `handle`, long-polling `GET /v1/shape` for new operations.
steps.say: Once it's up to date, the client switches into live mode. It calls the same endpoint again, this time with live set to true, the current offset, and the shape handle that identifies this subscription. The server holds the connection open, long polling, until new data arrives.

steps.title: New changes arrive live
steps.narration: When a row changes in **Postgres**, a new entry lands in the **Shape Log** and the held-open request returns it, advancing the `electric-offset`.
steps.say: From then on, whenever a row changes in Postgres a new entry lands in the shape log, the open request returns it, and the offset advances. The client reconnects and waits again, so it stays continuously up to date in real time.

chapters.title: Into a Local Collection
chapters.blurb: Materialize the shape log into a TanStack DB collection, read it reactively with useLiveQuery, and optionally persist in PGlite.

story.title: Into a Local Collection
story.subtitle: Sync Postgres into local clients over HTTP with Shapes

steps.title: Into a Local Collection
steps.narration: The raw shape log is low level. A client library materializes it into a **TanStack DB** collection you can query reactively.
steps.say: Consuming a log of operations by hand is low level work. So in practice you let a client library materialize that log into a local collection you can just query.
steps.coverSubtitle: Materialize into TanStack DB, read with useLiveQuery

steps.title: A ShapeStream consumes the log
steps.narration: A **ShapeStream** consumes the shape log from `GET /v1/shape`, handling offsets, the handle and live tailing for you.
steps.say: Underneath, a shape stream does the HTTP work from the last chapter for you. It consumes the shape log, manages the offset and the handle, and keeps the live connection going, so your code never touches those details.

steps.title: Configure a collection
steps.narration: `electricCollectionOptions` wires the stream to a collection: you pass `shapeOptions` with a `url` and `params.table`, plus a `getKey`.
steps.say: To turn that stream into a collection, you call electric collection options. You hand it shape options with the endpoint url and the table to sync, plus a get key function that tells it how to identify each row.

steps.title: Materialize a collection
steps.narration: `createCollection(electricCollectionOptions(...))` materializes the log into a local **TanStack DB collection** holding the current shape rows.
steps.say: Passing those options into create collection materializes the log into a Tan Stack D B collection. The collection holds the current value of every row in the shape, kept in sync as new operations arrive.

steps.title: Read with useLiveQuery
steps.narration: Components read the collection reactively with `useLiveQuery`, e.g. `q.from({ project }).where(({ project }) => eq(project.status, 'todo'))`.
steps.say: Your components then read the collection reactively with use live query. You write a small query over the collection, and whenever the underlying rows change, the query result updates and the component re-renders on its own.

steps.title: Optionally persist in PGlite
steps.narration: Optionally the collection can be held in a normalised store like **PGlite**, embeddable Postgres in the browser, for offline-capable local state.
steps.say: Optionally, instead of keeping the collection only in memory, you can persist it in P Glite, an embeddable Postgres that runs right in the browser. That gives you a durable local copy of the shape that survives reloads and works offline.

chapters.title: Writes Through Your API
chapters.blurb: Electric is read-path only: write optimistically, send the change to your own API, and let the confirmation sync back down the shape log.

story.title: Writes Through Your API
story.subtitle: Sync Postgres into local clients over HTTP with Shapes

steps.title: Writes Through Your API
steps.narration: Electric does *read-path* sync only. It deliberately doesn't get data back into Postgres for you — writes go through **your own API**.
steps.say: Here's the part that surprises people. Electric only does read path sync. It deliberately does not write data back into Postgres for you, so getting a change back to the database is your job.
steps.coverSubtitle: Read-path only: writes go back through your own write-path

steps.title: A local edit happens
steps.narration: A **component** edits the projects row — renaming a project. With Electric being read-only, this change still has to reach Postgres somehow.
steps.say: Say a component edits our projects row, renaming the project. Because Electric is read only, that edit has to travel back to Postgres through a path that you provide.

steps.title: Show it optimistically
steps.narration: First the app applies **optimistic state** — e.g. React's `useOptimistic` — so the new value shows immediately, taking the network off the write path.
steps.say: First, to keep things fast, the app applies the change as optimistic state, for instance with React's use optimistic hook. The new value shows on screen straight away, which takes the network off the write path and keeps the interface snappy.

steps.title: Send to your API
steps.narration: Then the write is sent to **your API** — a plain REST call, like the Node server in `patterns/1-online-writes`. This is the write-path you own.
steps.say: At the same time, the write is sent to your own API. It's just an ordinary REST call to a server you control, like the simple Node backend in the online writes pattern. This is the write path, and it's entirely yours.

steps.title: Your API writes Postgres
steps.narration: Your API validates and writes the change into **Postgres**, the durable source of truth, exactly as in any normal backend.
steps.say: Your API does what backends always do. It validates the request and writes the change into Postgres, the durable source of truth. Nothing here is specific to Electric, it's your normal write path.

steps.title: Confirmation syncs back
steps.narration: The committed change appears in the **Shape Log** and syncs back down to the app via Electric, which then discards the **optimistic state**.
steps.say: Now the loop closes. That committed change shows up in the shape log and syncs back down to the app over Electric's read path. When the confirmed value arrives, the app discards its optimistic state, because the real synced data has caught up.

chapters.title: The Whole Sync Loop
chapters.blurb: Re-trace one projects row: Postgres to a Shape, down the shape log into a TanStack DB collection, edited, and written back through your API.

story.title: The Whole Sync Loop
story.subtitle: Sync Postgres into local clients over HTTP with Shapes

steps.title: The Whole Sync Loop
steps.narration: Let's re-trace one **projects** row all the way around the loop: out of Postgres, into the client, edited, and back.
steps.say: Let's trace our one projects row all the way around the loop, from Postgres out to the client, through an edit, and back home again.
steps.coverSubtitle: One row: Postgres to shape to client, written back, and home again

steps.title: Defined as a Shape
steps.narration: The row lives in **Postgres** and is selected by a **Shape** — a table with an optional where clause and columns subset.
steps.say: It begins in Postgres. A shape selects it, defined by its table plus an optional where clause and an optional columns subset, carving out just the slice we care about.

steps.title: Down the shape log
steps.narration: The shape is served as a **Shape Log** over `GET /v1/shape` — an ordered stream of operations the client tails live.
steps.say: The shape is served as a shape log over the HTTP endpoint, an ordered stream of inserts, updates and deletes that the client reads and then tails live for real time changes.

steps.title: Into the local collection
steps.narration: A client materializes the log into a **TanStack DB collection**, and a **component** reads the row reactively with `useLiveQuery`.
steps.say: On the client, that log is materialized into a Tan Stack D B collection, and a component reads our row reactively with use live query, so the screen always reflects the latest synced value.

steps.title: Written back through your API
steps.narration: An edit goes optimistically local, then through **your API** to **Postgres** — the write-path you own, since Electric is read-only.
steps.say: When you edit the row, the change shows optimistically right away, then travels back through your own API into Postgres. Electric never writes for you, so that return trip is always your write path.

steps.title: The loop closes
steps.narration: The committed change re-enters the **Shape Log** and syncs back down to the **collection**, confirming the write. Postgres to shape to client to write, and home.
steps.say: And the loop closes. The committed change re enters the shape log and syncs back down into the collection, confirming the write and replacing the optimistic copy. Postgres, to shape, to client, to write, and all the way back home.
